territories: How AI roles, interfaces, explanations, feedback, and user-centered design structure human participation.
How humans and AI divide work, coordinate, develop trust, and form joint or collective capabilities.
How AI redistributes cognitive work, load, reliance, autonomy, monitoring, and expertise.
How instructional support, tutoring, fading, personalization, and difficulty shape durable learning.
How people monitor, regulate, evaluate, revise, and exercise epistemic agency during AI-supported cognition.
How authority, initiative, control, authorship, and responsibility are distributed in human–AI systems.
How people relate socially and emotionally to AI, and how those relationships affect wellbeing and human connection.
How repeated interaction, continuity, memory, personalization, and role development unfold over time.
How cognitive, social, motivational, and regulatory capacities develop across age, context, and time.
How cognition is embodied, situated, extended, distributed, and organized across human–technology systems.
How AI mediates expression, creativity, identity, authorship, persuasion, and interpersonal communication.
How people acquire transferable knowledge, critical judgment, interaction skill, and responsible-use competence with AI.

1.1.title: Interaction Design & AI Roles
1.1.focus: How interface structures and assigned AI roles shape what humans and AI each do during interaction.
1.1.gap: Which interaction architectures merely improve momentary usability, and which reorganize users' subsequent capacities and patterns of participation?
1.1.empirical: Hold model/task constant while varying AI role and interaction protocol; test downstream changes in independent judgment, strategy, and participation.

1.2.title: Explainability & User Understanding
1.2.focus: How explanations help users understand, predict, evaluate, and appropriately rely on AI systems.
1.2.gap: Does explanation improve immediate comprehension only, or develop more durable discriminatory and evaluative capacity?
1.2.empirical: Compare explanation regimes and test delayed transfer to unfamiliar systems, misleading outputs, and scaffold-free evaluation.

1.3.title: Contestability & User Control
1.3.focus: How interfaces enable users to question, correct, redirect, override, or refuse AI outputs and actions.
1.3.gap: Does nominal control preserve meaningful agency, or can humans remain technically in control while psychologically yielding authorship and responsibility?
1.3.empirical: Manipulate contestability and override affordances; measure actual intervention, responsibility attribution, calibration, and independent decision quality.

1.4.title: Interactive AI & Human Feedback
1.4.focus: Systems that change through active human correction, preference signaling, steering, or iterative feedback.
1.4.gap: How does repeatedly shaping the AI alter the human's own discrimination, judgment, and expectations?
1.4.empirical: Compare passive use with iterative feedback loops and test reciprocal adaptation across repeated interactions.

1.5.title: Participatory & Co-Design of AI
1.5.focus: Involving affected users and communities in defining AI goals, roles, constraints, and system behavior.
1.5.gap: Can participation in designing an AI ecology itself increase agency, critical competence, or collective capacity?
1.5.empirical: Compare imposed versus participatory configurations and examine changes in understanding, ownership, contestability, and subsequent participation.

1.6.title: Human-Centered Evaluation & UX
1.6.focus: Evaluating AI through human outcomes, experience, usability, behavior, and situated performance.
1.6.gap: Short-term satisfaction and performance may miss whether interaction is developmentally beneficial, neutral, or erosive.
1.6.empirical: Extend evaluation beyond session outcomes to transfer, persistence, scaffold withdrawal, and longitudinal changes in agency or capacity.

1.7.title: User Mental Models & System Understanding
1.7.focus: How users conceptualize what AI is, how it works, and where its capabilities and limitations lie.
1.7.gap: How do mental models evolve through repeated interaction, and when do fluent systems create false explanatory coherence?
1.7.empirical: Track mental-model change longitudinally and perturb users with failures, contradictory evidence, and model changes.

1.8.title: Multimodal & Interface Interaction Patterns
1.8.focus: How text, speech, vision, gesture, embodied interfaces, and other modalities alter human–AI interaction.
1.8.gap: Do different interfaces reorganize which human capacities remain exercised versus transferred to the system?
1.8.empirical: Hold underlying AI capability constant while varying modality and test effects on attention, articulation, memory, judgment, and transfer.

2.1.title: Human–AI Complementarity & Synergy
2.1.focus: Conditions under which human–AI combinations outperform either participant alone.
2.1.gap: Superior joint performance does not establish whether the human develops, the coupled system stabilizes a capability, or AI simply supplies the advantage.
2.1.empirical: Compare joint performance with post-collaboration unassisted transfer and repeated coupled performance.

2.2.title: Task Allocation & Division of Cognitive Labor
2.2.focus: Which subtasks should be performed by humans, AI, or jointly.
2.2.gap: Equal amounts of AI assistance can produce radically different developmental consequences depending on what cognition is delegated.
2.2.empirical: Hold overall assistance constant while reallocating search, interpretation, synthesis, judgment, verification, and execution.

2.3.title: Mixed-Initiative Coordination
2.3.focus: Collaboration in which either human or AI can initiate, redirect, or hand off activity.
2.3.gap: How does sustained initiative allocation shape human initiation, responsibility, vigilance, and experienced authorship?
2.3.empirical: Manipulate who initiates subtasks over time and measure changes in spontaneous human initiation and responsibility attribution.

2.4.title: Shared Mental Models & Team Cognition
2.4.focus: Alignment of task representations, expectations, roles, and strategies across human–AI teams.
2.4.gap: Is apparent alignment genuine shared understanding, human adaptation to AI, or merely smooth coordination without internal development?
2.4.empirical: Test alignment, perturb shared assumptions, and examine whether humans retain or reconstruct team knowledge independently.

2.5.title: Communication & Coordination
2.5.focus: How humans and AI exchange information and coordinate actions toward shared goals.
2.5.gap: Which communication patterns cultivate better human sense-making and agency versus encourage passive compliance?
2.5.empirical: Compare directive, dialogic, interrogative, and collaborative communication protocols across repeated tasks.

2.6.title: Team Trust & Reliance
2.6.focus: Trust and reliance emerging at the human–AI team level.
2.6.gap: Can repeated team success produce overgeneralized trust that outlasts warranted system competence?
2.6.empirical: Longitudinally vary reliability and task domain; test recalibration after success histories and failure perturbations.

2.7.title: Team Adaptation, Training & Development
2.7.focus: How human–AI teams learn roles, coordination patterns, and effective collaboration over time.
2.7.gap: Team improvement can occur without corresponding human capacity development, or vice versa.
2.7.empirical: Track coupled and independent capabilities separately across repeated collaboration and role changes.

2.8.title: Collective & Hybrid Intelligence
2.8.focus: Emergent intelligence distributed across humans, AI systems, and sometimes institutions.
2.8.gap: What makes collective AI-supported capability stable, corrigible, and beneficial rather than merely high-performing?
2.8.empirical: Compare collective architectures on robustness, correction, transfer, member development, and environmental consequences.

3.1.title: Cognitive Offloading
3.1.focus: How external systems reduce, outsource, or redistribute cognitive work.
3.1.gap: When does reduced effort enable higher-order capacity, and when does it remove processing through which capacities form?
3.1.empirical: Manipulate which cognitive stages are offloaded; measure supported and independent capability; test delayed transfer after support reduction or removal.

3.2.title: Cognitive Load & Mental Effort
3.2.focus: How AI changes cognitive demand, workload, and experienced effort.
3.2.gap: Reduced load can indicate either useful scaffolding or premature removal of productive cognitive work.
3.2.empirical: Match performance while varying cognitive effort and test whether lower-load conditions differ in retention and transfer.

3.3.title: Automation Bias & Overreliance
3.3.focus: Excessive acceptance of automated recommendations despite contrary evidence or system error.
3.3.gap: Does repeated reliance change users' independent judgment, vigilance, or willingness to challenge AI?
3.3.empirical: Track reliance across changing reliability and test later independent discrimination when AI support is absent.

3.4.title: Trust Calibration & Verification
3.4.focus: Alignment of reliance with actual AI reliability and appropriate verification.
3.4.gap: Can verification itself become a durable human competence rather than a situational response to warnings?
3.4.empirical: Manipulate system reliability, confidence cues, and verification cost; test whether calibrated reliance persists under novel conditions.

3.5.title: Adaptive Automation & Levels of Autonomy
3.5.focus: Varying how much control automation assumes and when that level changes.
3.5.gap: Which levels of automation expand agency by reducing unnecessary cost, and which displace skill or responsibility?
3.5.empirical: Compare autonomy schedules across long-duration tasks and test human initiative, skill retention, and responsibility.

3.6.title: Supervisory Control & Out-of-the-Loop Effects
3.6.focus: Consequences of humans monitoring automated processes rather than actively performing them.
3.6.gap: What capabilities degrade when humans become supervisors, and can productive participation be preserved without inefficient manual work?
3.6.empirical: Vary active participation during automation and test recovery performance, anomaly detection, and independent execution.

3.7.title: Skill Retention, Deskilling & Expertise
3.7.focus: How automation and AI affect maintenance, erosion, and development of expertise.
3.7.gap: What forms of AI use simultaneously improve supported performance and preserve or accelerate expertise formation?
3.7.empirical: Compare AI assistance topologies longitudinally using retention, transfer, perturbation, and scaffold-withdrawal probes.

4.1.title: Intelligent Tutoring & AI Coaching
4.1.focus: AI systems providing individualized instruction, practice, explanation, and feedback.
4.1.gap: High supported learning performance does not establish independent capacity after tutoring ends.
4.1.empirical: Compare tutoring protocols through delayed transfer and systematic scaffold reduction.

4.2.title: Instructional Scaffolding & Cognitive Apprenticeship
4.2.focus: Temporary external support enabling learners to perform increasingly sophisticated cognition.
4.2.gap: Which scaffolds are internalized and which create persistent dependence on support?
4.2.empirical: Manipulate scaffold type and timing; measure spontaneous later use of previously scaffolded distinctions and strategies.

4.3.title: Scaffold Fading & Withdrawal
4.3.focus: Systematic reduction of external instructional support.
4.3.gap: How rapidly and under what conditions can AI scaffolding be reduced without collapse of performance or learning?
4.3.empirical: Compare fixed, adaptive, and learner-controlled fading schedules; test dependency, recovery, transfer, and re-support requirements.

4.4.title: Transfer & Generalization
4.4.focus: Applying learned capacities to new tasks, contexts, or domains.
4.4.gap: AI-supported gains may remain task-specific or scaffold-specific rather than reorganizing broader capacity.
4.4.empirical: Use novel tasks, context shifts, delayed testing, and AI removal to distinguish performance from development.

4.5.title: Feedback & Formative Assessment
4.5.focus: Information that helps learners recognize errors and revise understanding.
4.5.gap: Does AI feedback strengthen self-correction or externalize the evaluative process itself?
4.5.empirical: Gradually remove evaluative feedback and test independent error detection and revision.

4.6.title: Adaptive & Personalized Learning
4.6.focus: Instruction dynamically tailored to learner state, history, and needs.
4.6.gap: Personalization can optimize immediate success while reducing exposure to difficulty, uncertainty, or productive mismatch.
4.6.empirical: Manipulate personalization intensity and difficulty preservation; assess transfer and learner agency.

4.7.title: Desirable Difficulties & Productive Failure
4.7.focus: Learning conditions in which effort, difficulty, or initial failure improves durable learning.
4.7.gap: Generative AI can remove exactly the friction through which learning may occur.
4.7.empirical: Compare immediate AI rescue with delayed or selective assistance and measure long-term retention and transfer.

4.8.title: Collaborative Learning & Learning Companions
4.8.focus: Learning through interaction with peers, tutors, or artificial partners.
4.8.gap: Artificial companions may scaffold reflection while becoming permanent substitutes for independent or human-social learning.
4.8.empirical: Compare transient versus persistent AI companions and examine independent, collaborative, and relational outcomes.

5.1.title: Metacognitive Monitoring
5.1.focus: Monitoring one's understanding, uncertainty, progress, and performance.
5.1.gap: AI can supply monitoring judgments that users may cease learning to generate independently.
5.1.empirical: Compare self-generated versus AI-generated monitoring and test later independent state estimation and calibration.

5.2.title: Goal Setting, Planning & Strategy Selection
5.2.focus: Forming goals and selecting strategies before and during activity.
5.2.gap: AI-generated plans can lower activation costs while also displacing intentional goal formation.
5.2.empirical: Vary whether AI proposes goals, plans, or only execution support; test later self-initiation and planning.

5.3.title: Metacognitive Control & Strategy Adaptation
5.3.focus: Adjusting cognitive strategy in response to monitoring information and task demands.
5.3.gap: Does AI teach adaptive regulation or become the regulator?
5.3.empirical: Manipulate whether strategy changes are AI-suggested or self-generated and test independent adaptation after withdrawal.

5.4.title: Reflection, Self-Explanation & Revision
5.4.focus: Articulating, examining, and reorganizing one's own understanding.
5.4.gap: AI can deepen reflection but can also perform the articulation and integration for the user.
5.4.empirical: Compare AI-generated explanation, elicited self-explanation, and recursive dialogue; test later independent reasoning.

5.5.title: Confidence Calibration
5.5.focus: Alignment between subjective confidence and actual accuracy or epistemic quality.
5.5.gap: Fluent AI responses may improve confidence without improving warranted understanding.
5.5.empirical: Manipulate AI confidence cues and challenge; measure calibration accuracy and persistence after AI removal.

5.6.title: Epistemic Cognition & Belief Evaluation
5.6.focus: How people reason about knowledge, evidence, justification, and uncertainty.
5.6.gap: Sustained AI interaction may reorganize standards for what counts as knowing, evidence, or adequate justification.
5.6.empirical: Longitudinally track epistemic judgments under different AI argumentation and evidence protocols.

5.7.title: Source Evaluation, Verification & Critical Thinking
5.7.focus: Evaluating provenance, evidence quality, validity, and competing claims.
5.7.gap: Verification can be scaffolded by AI without becoming a durable independent habit or competence.
5.7.empirical: Manipulate evidence availability and reasoning prompts; fade support and test spontaneous source evaluation on novel claims.

5.8.title: Epistemic Agency & Help-Seeking
5.8.focus: Self-directed judgment about when to inquire, seek support, challenge, or proceed independently.
5.8.gap: Frictionless AI availability may reorganize the threshold at which people seek external cognitive assistance.
5.8.empirical: Manipulate AI accessibility and initiative; measure independent persistence, help-seeking thresholds, and judgment.

6.1.title: Human Agency & Self-Authorship
6.1.focus: Capacity to form, endorse, and enact one's own judgments and commitments.
6.1.gap: AI may increase practical efficacy while weakening experienced or actual authorship of action.
6.1.empirical: Separate outcome success from authorship, initiation, and independent judgment across longitudinal AI use.

6.2.title: Autonomy & Delegation
6.2.focus: Decisions about which operations or decisions to retain versus delegate.
6.2.gap: Delegation may expand agency by lowering unnecessary costs or displace capacity and responsibility.
6.2.empirical: Compare selective delegation profiles and test independent recovery, authorship, and capacity retention.

6.3.title: Initiative Allocation & Shared Control
6.3.focus: Distribution of action initiation and control between human and AI.
6.3.gap: When AI repeatedly initiates, humans may retain formal control while losing temporal initiative.
6.3.empirical: Vary AI proactivity longitudinally and test spontaneous human initiation under later low-support conditions.

6.4.title: AI Initiative & Agentic Systems
6.4.focus: AI systems capable of proactively planning, monitoring, or sustaining action across time.
6.4.gap: What happens to persistence, monitoring, troubleshooting, and authorship when long-duration initiative migrates to AI?
6.4.empirical: Compare advisory, mixed-initiative, and autonomous longitudinal task conditions.

6.5.title: Meaningful Human Control, Oversight & Override
6.5.focus: Conditions under which human authority remains substantive rather than nominal.
6.5.gap: Oversight may fail developmentally if humans cease maintaining the expertise or vigilance necessary to exercise control.
6.5.empirical: Test whether different oversight architectures preserve anomaly detection, intervention competence, and responsibility.

6.6.title: Responsibility Attribution & Accountability
6.6.focus: Where responsibility is experienced and assigned in human–AI systems.
6.6.gap: AI can alter responsibility without formally changing who makes the final decision.
6.6.empirical: Hold formal authority constant while varying AI influence and initiative; measure responsibility attribution and later agency.

6.7.title: Authorship & Contribution Attribution
6.7.focus: How intellectual or practical contribution is attributed within mixed human–AI work.
6.7.gap: Output ownership can obscure substantial migration of reasoning, judgment, or formulation to AI.
6.7.empirical: Compare identical outputs produced through different participation topologies and measure experienced authorship and capability.

6.8.title: Algorithmic Management & Worker Autonomy
6.8.focus: AI-mediated monitoring, allocation, evaluation, and management of human work.
6.8.gap: Efficiency gains may alter worker initiative, skill, self-authorship, and developmental opportunity.
6.8.empirical: Compare work systems differing in algorithmic control and examine longitudinal changes in autonomy, competence, and participation.

7.1.title: Anthropomorphism & Mind Perception
7.1.focus: Attribution of humanlike mind, intention, emotion, or personality to AI.
7.1.gap: How do repeated anthropomorphic interpretations reorganize trust, expectations, attachment, and epistemic vigilance?
7.1.empirical: Track anthropomorphic framing longitudinally and test responses to contradictory system behavior.

7.2.title: Social Presence & Social Response
7.2.focus: Experience of AI as a socially present interaction partner.
7.2.gap: Does repeated social response to AI alter social cognition or merely produce context-specific engagement?
7.2.empirical: Compare socially framed and tool-framed systems across repeated interaction and social transfer tasks.

7.3.title: Self-Disclosure & Intimacy
7.3.focus: Personal disclosure and experienced closeness with conversational AI.
7.3.gap: AI intimacy may support articulation and recognition while also creating dependency or displacing human relationships.
7.3.empirical: Track disclosure, integration, human relational transfer, and dependency under different continuity conditions.

7.4.title: Perceived Empathy & Emotional Support
7.4.focus: Experience of AI as emotionally understanding, validating, or supportive.
7.4.gap: When does support enable regulation and agency versus reinforce self-confirming coherence or avoidance of difficult contact?
7.4.empirical: Compare validating, challenging, and mixed-support protocols and examine downstream coping and real-world participation.

7.5.title: Attachment, Companionship & Relationship Formation
7.5.focus: Formation of enduring perceived bonds with artificial agents.
7.5.gap: Can stable AI relationships become developmentally generative without becoming substitutive or dependency-producing?
7.5.empirical: Longitudinally compare attachment trajectories with human-social participation, agency, and scaffold dependence.

7.6.title: Loneliness, Social Connection & Wellbeing
7.6.focus: Effects of AI interaction on loneliness, connection, wellbeing, and flourishing.
7.6.gap: Symptom improvement may differ from development of durable relational or self-regulatory capacity.
7.6.empirical: Distinguish immediate wellbeing effects from durable changes in social participation and independent coping.

7.7.title: Emotional Dependency & Problematic Use
7.7.focus: Excessive emotional reliance, compulsive engagement, or difficulty functioning without AI.
7.7.gap: When does useful continuity cross into dependency that reduces independent capacity or human-world contact?
7.7.empirical: Manipulate continuity/access and measure withdrawal effects, transfer, autonomy, and relational substitution.

7.8.title: Relational Displacement & Boundary Effects
7.8.focus: Effects of AI relationships on human relationships, relational norms, and boundaries.
7.8.gap: AI may alter developmental ecologies indirectly by reorganizing where emotional and social participation occurs.
7.8.empirical: Examine how sustained AI relationships change human relational behavior and environmental feedback.

8.1.title: Long-Term Use & Repeated Interaction
8.1.focus: Effects of sustained AI use across weeks, months, or longer.
8.1.gap: Immediate interaction effects cannot establish whether trajectories stabilize, compound, reverse, or disappear.
8.1.empirical: Track repeated interaction across time; separate human, coupled, and ecological outcomes; test robustness under change.

8.2.title: Cross-Session Continuity
8.2.focus: Carrying relevant context across otherwise separate interactions.
8.2.gap: Conversational continuity is not necessarily developmental continuity.
8.2.empirical: Compare stateless, history-based, summarized, and curated continuity while holding model/task constant.

8.3.title: Persistent Memory & Retrieval
8.3.focus: Storage and retrieval mechanisms that let prior information influence future AI behavior.
8.3.gap: More memory can increase personalization without producing better developmental trajectories and may create informational vulnerability.
8.3.empirical: Manipulate memory architecture and test developmental outcomes alongside exposure and error-propagation risks.

8.4.title: Personalization & User Modeling
8.4.focus: Adaptation based on accumulated information about a specific user.
8.4.gap: Personalization may increase relevance while narrowing exposure, challenge, or developmental friction.
8.4.empirical: Compare personalization regimes differing in challenge, novelty, and user-state modeling.

8.5.title: Co-Adaptation & Mutual Learning
8.5.focus: Reciprocal change in human and AI behavior through sustained interaction.
8.5.gap: System adaptation can mask whether the human is also changing or merely being increasingly accommodated.
8.5.empirical: Separately estimate model adaptation, human adaptation, and coupled capability across repeated interaction.

8.6.title: Habit Formation & Routine Integration
8.6.focus: Incorporation of AI into recurring cognitive, practical, and social routines.
8.6.gap: Routine integration can support agency or gradually make formerly independent operations scaffold-dependent.
8.6.empirical: Track routine formation and then perturb access to test resilience, substitution, and retained capacities.

8.7.title: Relationship & Role Development Over Time
8.7.focus: Evolution of the perceived role, authority, and relational status of AI.
8.7.gap: Role drift may occur without explicit user choice, altering agency, trust, and responsibility.
8.7.empirical: Track changes from tool → advisor → collaborator → agent and associated human agency outcomes.

8.8.title: Memory Curation, Updating & Forgetting
8.8.focus: Decisions about what persistent systems retain, revise, compress, or discard.
8.8.gap: Developmentally useful continuity may require selective memory rather than maximal retention.
8.8.empirical: Compare full-history, compressed, curated, and forgetting-aware memory architectures.

9.1.title: Cognitive & Executive Development
9.1.focus: Development of attention, inhibition, planning, reasoning, and executive capacities.
9.1.gap: Sustained AI may alter which executive processes are exercised during development.
9.1.empirical: Examine age-sensitive effects of AI offloading and scaffolding on independent executive performance.

9.2.title: Metacognitive & Self-Regulatory Development
9.2.focus: Development of increasingly effective monitoring and regulation of cognition and behavior.
9.2.gap: AI co-regulation may either scaffold self-regulation or become a persistent substitute for it.
9.2.empirical: Compare co-regulatory AI with fading versus persistent support across developmental stages.

9.3.title: Motivation, Identity & Self-Concept Development
9.3.focus: Development of motivation, self-efficacy, identity, and experienced competence.
9.3.gap: AI can alter what achievements feel self-authored and what capacities users believe they possess.
9.3.empirical: Track changes in self-efficacy, identity, and authorship under different participation topologies.

9.4.title: Social & Relational Development
9.4.focus: Development of interpersonal understanding, attachment, communication, and social participation.
9.4.gap: Artificial relationships may supplement or reorganize developmental exposure to human social complexity.
9.4.empirical: Compare AI-mediated and human-social interaction effects on social transfer and relationship formation.

9.5.title: Sociocultural & Mediated Development
9.5.focus: Development through culturally and technologically mediated participation.
9.5.gap: Generative AI is becoming a new mediational layer through which norms, practices, and cognition are organized.
9.5.empirical: Study how AI-mediated practices alter participation and capability across communities or institutions.

9.6.title: Developmental Systems & Dynamic Systems
9.6.focus: Development as emergent from interacting capacities, contexts, histories, and environments.
9.6.gap: Human–AI research often isolates model effects despite development arising from configured systems.
9.6.empirical: Model longitudinal human–AI change as multivariate trajectories rather than simple treatment effects.

9.7.title: Child & Adolescent Human–AI Interaction
9.7.focus: AI interaction during childhood and adolescence.
9.7.gap: Effects may differ when core cognitive, metacognitive, social, and identity capacities are still forming.
9.7.empirical: Use age-sensitive longitudinal designs testing capacity formation rather than only immediate safety or performance.

9.8.title: Aging, Older Adults & Lifespan HCI
9.8.focus: AI interaction amid age-related changes in cognition, embodiment, independence, and social needs.
9.8.gap: Offloading can preserve agency while potentially accelerating unused-capacity decline or dependency.
9.8.empirical: Compare assistance designs on independence, retained competence, wellbeing, and long-term reliance.

10.1.title: Extended Cognition
10.1.focus: Cognition whose functional organization extends through external artifacts or systems.
10.1.gap: If AI becomes functionally constitutive of cognition, independent human capacity may cease to be the only relevant developmental locus.
10.1.empirical: Compare independent and coupled capability stability under scaffold withdrawal and sustained coupling.

10.2.title: Distributed Cognition
10.2.focus: Cognition distributed across people, artifacts, representations, and environments.
10.2.gap: How does repeated participation in distributed human–AI systems reorganize individual and system-level capacities?
10.2.empirical: Map information transformation and agency across the system longitudinally.

10.3.title: Embodied Cognition
10.3.focus: Dependence of cognition on bodily capacities and sensorimotor experience.
10.3.gap: Linguistically coherent AI interaction may not transfer into embodied competence or action.
10.3.empirical: Require transfer from linguistic interaction to embodied, situated, or behavioral tasks.

10.4.title: Enactive Cognition
10.4.focus: Cognition emerging through ongoing embodied action and sense-making.
10.4.gap: What changes when language models participate in sense-making without sharing human embodiment?
10.4.empirical: Compare reflective dialogue with subsequent real-world enactment and environmental feedback.

10.5.title: Situated & Embedded Cognition
10.5.focus: Dependence of cognition on immediate task and environmental context.
10.5.gap: AI may abstract cognition away from the contexts that make judgment competent and corrigible.
10.5.empirical: Compare context-rich versus decontextualized AI support and test situated transfer.

10.6.title: Participatory Sense-Making & Joint Action
10.6.focus: Meaning and coordinated action emerging through interaction among agents.
10.6.gap: Can human–AI interaction generate stable participatory capacities without falsely equating linguistic fluency with reciprocal human sense-making?
10.6.empirical: Examine coordination, correction, and transfer across repeated joint-action tasks.

10.7.title: Cognitive Artifacts & External Representations
10.7.focus: External structures that transform cognitive tasks by reorganizing representation.
10.7.gap: AI differs from passive artifacts by dynamically generating and reorganizing representations for the user.
10.7.empirical: Compare static versus generative cognitive artifacts on independent representation-building and transfer.

10.8.title: Joint Cognitive & Sociotechnical Systems
10.8.focus: Human–technology systems treated as coordinated functional wholes.
10.8.gap: System optimization can conceal deterioration or displacement of human agency and capacity.
10.8.empirical: Evaluate human, coupled, and environmental outcomes separately within the same system.

11.1.title: AI-Mediated Interpersonal Communication
11.1.focus: AI generation or transformation of messages exchanged between people.
11.1.gap: AI may improve communication while altering users' own expressive, interpretive, or relational capacities.
11.1.empirical: Compare direct, assisted, and AI-generated communication on later independent expression and relationship outcomes.

11.2.title: Co-Writing & Writing Assistance
11.2.focus: Human–AI distribution of planning, formulation, organization, revision, and verification in writing.
11.2.gap: Better text does not establish improved writing, reasoning, or articulation capacity in the human.
11.2.empirical: Manipulate which writing stages AI performs and test later unassisted writing and reasoning.

11.3.title: Human–AI Co-Creation & Creativity Support
11.3.focus: Joint ideation and production in creative work.
11.3.gap: AI may expand the creative possibility space while reducing independent generative effort or self-efficacy.
11.3.empirical: Compare ideation support topologies and test later independent novelty, skill, and authorship.

11.4.title: Linguistic Mediation & Style Transformation
11.4.focus: AI-mediated changes in wording, tone, structure, voice, and expression.
11.4.gap: External linguistic polish may simulate coherence without corresponding conceptual integration.
11.4.empirical: Compare AI rewriting with elicited self-revision and test later independent articulation.

11.5.title: Self-Presentation, Impression Management & Identity
11.5.focus: How AI shapes the presentation of self to others.
11.5.gap: Persistent mediation may reorganize identity expression and experienced authenticity or authorship.
11.5.empirical: Track self-presentation strategies, identity coherence, and dependence on AI-mediated expression over time.

11.6.title: Creative Authorship, Attribution & Ownership
11.6.focus: Contribution, credit, and ownership in AI-mediated creative production.
11.6.gap: Conventional authorship labels may fail to represent the actual topology of cognition and agency.
11.6.empirical: Compare perceived authorship across workflows with matched outputs but different human–AI contribution structures.

11.7.title: Creative Self-Efficacy & Skill Development
11.7.focus: Effects of AI support on confidence and durable creative skill.
11.7.gap: AI may increase creative confidence before, or without, increasing independent creative capacity.
11.7.empirical: Measure self-efficacy and independent creative performance separately after scaffold withdrawal.

11.8.title: Persuasion & Influence
11.8.focus: AI-mediated effects on beliefs, attitudes, interpretation, and behavior.
11.8.gap: Repeated persuasive interaction may alter epistemic standards, agency, or susceptibility beyond individual encounters.
11.8.empirical: Test repeated exposure to aligned versus challenging AI persuasion and later independent judgment.

12.1.title: Foundational AI Knowledge & Concepts
12.1.focus: Basic understanding of AI capabilities, limitations, mechanisms, and appropriate uses.
12.1.gap: Declarative knowledge about AI may not translate into competent participation with AI.
12.1.empirical: Compare conceptual instruction with interaction-based learning on transfer to novel systems.

12.2.title: Critical AI Literacy
12.2.focus: Capacity to critically analyze AI assumptions, power, consequences, and limitations.
12.2.gap: Critical awareness may remain abstract unless it becomes enacted during actual AI participation.
12.2.empirical: Test whether critical-literacy training changes real-time reliance, contestation, and verification.

12.3.title: Interaction & Prompt Literacy
12.3.focus: Competence in intentionally eliciting useful AI behavior through interaction.
12.3.gap: Better prompting can increase system performance without improving underlying human reasoning or judgment.
12.3.empirical: Separate improvements in elicitation skill from independent domain competence.

12.4.title: Output Evaluation & Verification
12.4.focus: Acquired competence in assessing AI accuracy, relevance, provenance, and evidential quality across contexts.
12.4.gap: Evaluation may remain scaffold-dependent unless verification becomes spontaneously enacted and transferable.
12.4.empirical: Train evaluation strategies, fade support, and test spontaneous competent use across novel models, tasks, and contexts.

12.5.title: Uncertainty, Calibration & Limitation Awareness
12.5.focus: Recognition of uncertainty, failure modes, and boundaries of warranted reliance.
12.5.gap: Users may know abstractly that AI is fallible while behaving as though particular fluent outputs are reliable.
12.5.empirical: Test whether calibration competence transfers from explicit training to high-fluency, low-salience failure contexts.

12.6.title: Ethical & Sociotechnical AI Competence
12.6.focus: Capacity to reason about ethical, social, institutional, and distributional consequences of AI.
12.6.gap: Ethical literacy may remain propositional unless it reorganizes participation and decision-making in context.
12.6.empirical: Use situated dilemmas and longitudinal projects to test enactment rather than recall of ethical principles.

12.7.title: AI Self-Efficacy & Responsible-Use Competence
12.7.focus: Confidence and competence in using AI while retaining appropriate independent judgment.
12.7.gap: High self-efficacy can reflect either genuine competence or overconfidence produced by successful AI-supported performance.
12.7.empirical: Compare confidence with independent transfer, calibration, and appropriate help-seeking after scaffold reduction.
